claim: A unilateral injury of the hindlimb sensorimotor cortex of rats with completely transected thoracic spinal cord produces hindlimb postural asymmetry with contralateral flexion within 3 hr.
source: Brain injuries can interrupt descending neural pathways that convey motor commands from the cortex to spinal motoneurons. Here, we demonstrate that a unilateral injury of the hindlimb sensorimotor cortex of rats with completely transected thoracic spinal cord produces hindlimb postural asymmetry with contralateral flexion and asymmetric hindlimb withdrawal reflexes within 3 hr, as well as asymmetry in gene expression patterns in the lumbar spinal cord.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including measurements of hindlimb postural asymmetry and statistical analyses showing significant differences between UBI and sham surgery groups.

claim: A unilateral injury of the hindlimb sensorimotor cortex of rats with completely transected thoracic spinal cord produces asymmetric hindlimb withdrawal reflexes within 3 hr.
source: Brain injuries can interrupt descending neural pathways that convey motor commands from the cortex to spinal motoneurons. Here, we demonstrate that a unilateral injury of the hindlimb sensorimotor cortex of rats with completely transected thoracic spinal cord produces hindlimb postural asymmetry with contralateral flexion and asymmetric hindlimb withdrawal reflexes within 3 hr, as well as asymmetry in gene expression patterns in the lumbar spinal cord.
evidence: The claim is supported by EMG recordings and statistical analyses presented in Figure 2 and related text, showing asymmetric withdrawal reflexes in UBI rats compared to sham surgery controls.

claim: A unilateral injury of the hindlimb sensorimotor cortex of rats with completely transected thoracic spinal cord produces asymmetry in gene expression patterns in the lumbar spinal cord within 3 hr.
source: Brain injuries can interrupt descending neural pathways that convey motor commands from the cortex to spinal motoneurons. Here, we demonstrate that a unilateral injury of the hindlimb sensorimotor cortex of rats with completely transected thoracic spinal cord produces hindlimb postural asymmetry with contralateral flexion and asymmetric hindlimb withdrawal reflexes within 3 hr, as well as asymmetry in gene expression patterns in the lumbar spinal cord.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data and correlation analyses presented in Figure 3 and supplementary figures, showing changes in gene expression asymmetry and coordination between left and right spinal cord halves.

claim: The injury-induced postural effects were abolished by hypophysectomy.
source: The injury-induced postural effects were abolished by hypophysectomy and were mimicked by transfusion of serum from animals with brain injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4A showing that hypophysectomized rats did not develop hindlimb postural asymmetry after UBI, with statistical analyses confirming no significant difference from sham surgery controls.

claim: The injury-induced postural effects were mimicked by transfusion of serum from animals with brain injury.
source: The injury-induced postural effects were abolished by hypophysectomy and were mimicked by transfusion of serum from animals with brain injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing that serum from UBI rats induced hindlimb postural asymmetry when administered to naive rats with transected spinal cords.

claim: Administration of β-endorphin induced side-specific hindlimb responses in naive animals.
source: Administration of the pituitary neurohormones β-endorphin or Arg-vasopressin-induced side-specific hindlimb responses in naive animals, while antagonists of the opioid and vasopressin receptors blocked hindlimb postural asymmetry in rats with brain injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4C showing that intravenous administration of β-endorphin induced hindlimb postural asymmetry with right hindlimb flexion in rats with transected spinal cords.

claim: Administration of Arg-vasopressin induced side-specific hindlimb responses in naive animals.
source: Administration of the pituitary neurohormones β-endorphin or Arg-vasopressin-induced side-specific hindlimb responses in naive animals, while antagonists of the opioid and vasopressin receptors blocked hindlimb postural asymmetry in rats with brain injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2 showing that Arg-vasopressin administration induced hindlimb postural asymmetry with right hindlimb flexion in rats with transected spinal cords.

claim: Antagonists of the opioid receptors blocked hindlimb postural asymmetry in rats with brain injury.
source: Administration of the pituitary neurohormones β-endorphin or Arg-vasopressin-induced side-specific hindlimb responses in naive animals, while antagonists of the opioid and vasopressin receptors blocked hindlimb postural asymmetry in rats with brain injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4D and 4E showing that naloxone, an opioid receptor antagonist, inhibited hindlimb postural asymmetry formation in UBI rats and in rats treated with UBI serum.

claim: Antagonists of the vasopressin receptors blocked hindlimb postural asymmetry in rats with brain injury.
source: Administration of the pituitary neurohormones β-endorphin or Arg-vasopressin-induced side-specific hindlimb responses in naive animals, while antagonists of the opioid and vasopressin receptors blocked hindlimb postural asymmetry in rats with brain injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4D and 4E showing that SSR-149415, a vasopressin V1B receptor antagonist, inhibited hindlimb postural asymmetry formation in UBI rats and in rats treated with UBI serum.

claim: Side-specific humoral signaling may add to postural and reflex asymmetries seen after brain injury in addition to motor pathways descending from the brain to spinal circuits.
source: Thus, in addition to the well-established involvement of motor pathways descending from the brain to spinal circuits, the side-specific humoral signaling may also add to postural and reflex asymmetries seen after brain injury.
evidence: The claim is based on the integration of multiple experimental findings showing that UBI effects persist after spinal cord transection, are abolished by hypophysectomy, can be mimicked by serum transfer, and are blocked by neurohormone receptor antagonists.

claim: Brain lesions can interrupt descending neural pathways that convey motor commands from the cerebral cortex to motoneurons located in the brain stem and anterior horn of the spinal grey matter.
source: Brain lesions can interrupt descending neural pathways that convey motor commands from the cerebral cortex to motoneurons located in the brain stem and anterior horn of the spinal grey matter (Cai et al., 2019; Kuypers, 1981; Lemon, 2008; Purves et al., 2001; Smith et al., 2017; Tan et al., 2012; Zörner et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature on motor pathways and their disruption following brain lesions.

claim: Brain injury-induced motor deficits typically develop on the contralateral side of the body.
source: Brain injury-induced motor deficits typically develop on the contralateral side of the body and include motor weakness, loss of voluntary movements, spasticity, asymmetric limb reflexes, and abnormal posture.
evidence: The claim is based on established clinical and experimental knowledge about the contralateral organization of motor pathways, supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Brain injury-induced motor deficits include motor weakness, loss of voluntary movements, spasticity, asymmetric limb reflexes, and abnormal posture.
source: Brain injury-induced motor deficits typically develop on the contralateral side of the body and include motor weakness, loss of voluntary movements, spasticity, asymmetric limb reflexes, and abnormal posture.
evidence: The claim is based on established clinical knowledge about motor deficits following brain injury, supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Motor deficits after brain injury are related to impaired signaling through the descending motor tracts and to deafferentation-induced spinal neuroplasticity.
source: Evidence suggests that these deficits are related to the impaired signaling through the descending motor tracts and to deafferentation-induced spinal neuroplasticity (Cai et al., 2019; Deliagina et al., 2014; Kanagal and Muir, 2009; Küchler et al., 2002; Li and Francisco, 2015; Morris and Whishaw, 2016; Tan et al., 2012; Whishaw et al., 1998; Zelenin et al., 2016; Zörner et al., 2014; Zörner et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies investigating mechanisms of motor deficits after brain injury.

claim: A unilateral brain injury induces hindlimb postural asymmetry with contralesional limb flexion in animal experiments.
source: In animal experiments, a unilateral brain injury (UBI) induces hindlimb postural asymmetry (HL-PA) with contralesional limb flexion and asymmetry of the hindlimb withdrawal reflexes (Watanabe et al., 2021; Watanabe et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors and experimental data presented in the current manuscript.

claim: A unilateral brain injury induces asymmetry of the hindlimb withdrawal reflexes in animal experiments.
source: In animal experiments, a unilateral brain injury (UBI) induces hindlimb postural asymmetry (HL-PA) with contralesional limb flexion and asymmetry of the hindlimb withdrawal reflexes (Watanabe et al., 2021; Watanabe et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and experimental data presented in the current manuscript showing asymmetric withdrawal reflexes after UBI.

claim: Lateral hemisection of the spinal cord impairs postural functions.
source: Consistently, lateral hemisection of the spinal cord impairs postural functions (Zelenin et al., 2016) and enhances monosynaptic and polysynaptic hindlimb reflexes on the ipsilesional side (Hultborn and Malmsten, 1983a; Hultborn and Malmsten, 1983b; Malmsten, 1983; Rossignol and Frigon, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study by Zelenin et al., 2016.

claim: Lateral hemisection of the spinal cord enhances monosynaptic and polysynaptic hindlimb reflexes on the ipsilesional side.
source: Consistently, lateral hemisection of the spinal cord impairs postural functions (Zelenin et al., 2016) and enhances monosynaptic and polysynaptic hindlimb reflexes on the ipsilesional side (Hultborn and Malmsten, 1983a; Hultborn and Malmsten, 1983b; Malmsten, 1983; Rossignol and Frigon, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies investigating reflex changes after spinal cord hemisection.

claim: Asymmetry in posture and reflexes persists after complete transection of the spinal cord.
source: Asymmetry in posture and reflexes persists after complete transection of the spinal cord (Rossignol and Frigon, 2011; Watanabe et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and experimental data in the current manuscript showing that UBI-induced asymmetries persist after spinal cord transection.

claim: Opioid peptides may induce the formation of hindlimb postural asymmetry in rats with intact brains.
source: Analysis of neurotransmitter mechanisms demonstrates that opioid peptides and Arg-vasopressin may induce the formation of HL-PA in rats with intact brains (Bakalkin et al., 1981; Bakalkin et al., 1986; Chazov et al., 1981; Klement'ev et al., 1986; Watanabe et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating that opioid peptides can induce hindlimb postural asymmetry.

claim: Arg-vasopressin may induce the formation of hindlimb postural asymmetry in rats with intact brains.
source: Analysis of neurotransmitter mechanisms demonstrates that opioid peptides and Arg-vasopressin may induce the formation of HL-PA in rats with intact brains (Bakalkin et al., 1981; Bakalkin et al., 1986; Chazov et al., 1981; Klement'ev et al., 1986; Watanabe et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and experimental data in the current manuscript showing that Arg-vasopressin induces hindlimb postural asymmetry.

claim: The κ-opioid agonists dynorphin, bremazocine and U-50,488 induce flexion of the left hindlimb.
source: Either the left or the right hindlimb can be flexed, depending on the compound injected. The κ-opioid agonists dynorphin, bremazocine and U-50,488, as well as the preferential endogenous µ-opioid agonist Met-enkephalin, induce flexion of the left hindlimb, whereas the δ-opioid agonist Leu-enkephalin and Arg-vasopressin cause the right limb to flex.
evidence: The claim is based on previous studies cited in the manuscript demonstrating side-specific effects of different opioid agonists.

claim: Met-enkephalin induces flexion of the left hindlimb.
source: Either the left or the right hindlimb can be flexed, depending on the compound injected. The κ-opioid agonists dynorphin, bremazocine and U-50,488, as well as the preferential endogenous µ-opioid agonist Met-enkephalin, induce flexion of the left hindlimb, whereas the δ-opioid agonist Leu-enkephalin and Arg-vasopressin cause the right limb to flex.
evidence: The claim is based on previous studies cited in the manuscript demonstrating side-specific effects of Met-enkephalin.

claim: The δ-opioid agonist Leu-enkephalin causes the right limb to flex.
source: Either the left or the right hindlimb can be flexed, depending on the compound injected. The κ-opioid agonists dynorphin, bremazocine and U-50,488, as well as the preferential endogenous µ-opioid agonist Met-enkephalin, induce flexion of the left hindlimb, whereas the δ-opioid agonist Leu-enkephalin and Arg-vasopressin cause the right limb to flex.
evidence: The claim is based on previous studies cited in the manuscript demonstrating side-specific effects of Leu-enkephalin.

claim: Arg-vasopressin causes the right limb to flex.
source: Either the left or the right hindlimb can be flexed, depending on the compound injected. The κ-opioid agonists dynorphin, bremazocine and U-50,488, as well as the preferential endogenous µ-opioid agonist Met-enkephalin, induce flexion of the left hindlimb, whereas the δ-opioid agonist Leu-enkephalin and Arg-vasopressin cause the right limb to flex.
evidence: The claim is supported by previous studies cited in the manuscript and experimental data in the current study showing that Arg-vasopressin induces right hindlimb flexion.

claim: In the rat spinal cord, the expression of the opioid receptors and their co-expression patterns are different between the left and right sides.
source: The left-right side-specific neurohormonal effects may be induced through lateralized receptors. Indeed, in the rat spinal cord, the expression of the opioid receptors and their co-expression patterns are different between the left and right sides (Kononenko et al., 2017; Watanabe et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors demonstrating lateralized expression of opioid receptors in the rat spinal cord.

claim: The spinal cord was transected at the T2-T3 level before the hindlimb representation area of the sensorimotor cortex was ablated.
source: The spinal cord was transected at the T2-T3 level and then the hindlimb representation area of the sensorimotor cortex was ablated (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental procedure used in the study, which is documented in the methods section and illustrated in figures.

claim: HL-PA was analyzed within 3 hr after the UBI by both the hands-on and hands-off methods of hindlimb stretching.
source: HL-PA was analyzed within 3 hr after the UBI by both the hands-on and hands-off methods of hindlimb stretching followed by photographic and / or visual recording of the asymmetry in animals under pentobarbital anesthesia (for details, see 'Materials and methods' and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods used to assess hindlimb postural asymmetry, which are detailed in the methods section and supplementary figures.

claim: UBI produced HL-PA with contralesional hindlimb flexion within 3 hr after the UBI in rats with intact spinal cord.
source: Control experiments demonstrated that this injury produced HL-PA with contralesional hindlimb flexion within 3 hr after the UBI in rats with intact spinal cord (Figure 1F–H; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D), and contralesional hindlimb motor deficits in the beam-walking and ladder rung tests (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1F-H and supplementary figures showing hindlimb postural asymmetry in rats with intact spinal cords after UBI.

claim: UBI produced contralesional hindlimb motor deficits in the beam-walking and ladder rung tests.
source: Control experiments demonstrated that this injury produced HL-PA with contralesional hindlimb flexion within 3 hr after the UBI in rats with intact spinal cord (Figure 1F–H; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D), and contralesional hindlimb motor deficits in the beam-walking and ladder rung tests (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F showing increased errors in the contralesional hindlimb in behavioral tests.

claim: In rats with transected spinal cords, the UBI induced HL-PA with contralesional hindlimb flexion.
source: Strikingly, in the rats with transected spinal cords the UBI also induced HL-PA (Figure 1C–E). The HL-PA developed within 3 hr after the brain injury. Its size and probability were much greater than in rats with sham surgery (Left UBI, n = 31; Right UBI, n = 15; sham surgery, n = 29). An unanticipated observation was that in rats with HL-PA, the hindlimb was flexed on the contralesional side.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1C-E showing that UBI induced hindlimb postural asymmetry with contralesional flexion even after complete spinal cord transection.

claim: The left or right hindlimb flexion was induced by the right and left UBI, respectively, in rats with transected spinal cords.
source: The left or right hindlimb flexion was induced by the right and left UBI, respectively (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,C; Figure 1—figure supplement 4B,C,F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in multiple figures showing the side-specific pattern of hindlimb flexion corresponding to the side of brain injury.

claim: Both Wistar rats and Sprague Dawley rats developed HL-PA with hindlimb flexion on the contralesional side after UBI and spinal cord transection.
source: Both Wistar rats (Figure 1D–E; Figure 1—figure supplement 3, 4F-I) and Sprague Dawley rats (Figure 1—figure supplements 4B–E and 5) that were used in further molecular and electrophysiological experiments, respectively, developed HL-PA with hindlimb flexion on the contralesional side.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from two different rat strains showing consistent results across genetic backgrounds.

claim: After excision of a 3-4 mm spinal segment at the T2-T3 level, the left-side UBI induced hindlimb postural asymmetry with the right limb flexion.
source: To ensure the completeness of the transection, a 3–4 mm spinal segment was excised at the T2-T3 level in a subset of rats (Figure 1—figure supplement 5). After the excision, the left-side UBI-induced hindlimb postural asymmetry with the right limb flexion that replicated the other findings.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5 showing that even with complete removal of a spinal segment, UBI still induced hindlimb postural asymmetry.

claim: HL-PA formation in animals with transected spinal cord is mediated through a pathway that operates in parallel with the descending neural tracts.
source: We conclude that HL-PA formation in animals with transected spinal cord is mediated through a pathway that operates in parallel with the descending neural tracts and assures the development of contralesional flexion.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental finding that UBI induces hindlimb postural asymmetry even after complete spinal cord transection, which eliminates descending neural pathways.

claim: UBI in rats with transected spinal cords produces asymmetry in withdrawal reflexes.
source: Thus, in rats with transected spinal cord, UBI, but not sham surgery, induced asymmetry in withdrawal reflexes.
evidence: The claim is supported by EMG data presented in Figure 2 showing asymmetric withdrawal reflexes in UBI rats compared to sham surgery controls.

claim: The number of spikes of the extensor digitorum longus muscle was higher on the contra vs. ipsilateral side in the UBI rats with transected spinal cord.
source: The number of spikes of both flexor muscles, the extensor digitorum longus and semitendinosus was higher on the contra vs. ipsilateral side in the UBI rats.
evidence: The claim is supported by EMG data and statistical analyses presented in Figure 2D showing a 3.5-fold higher number of spikes in the contralesional extensor digitorum longus muscle.

claim: The number of spikes of the semitendinosus muscle was higher on the contra vs. ipsilateral side in the UBI rats with transected spinal cord.
source: The number of spikes of both flexor muscles, the extensor digitorum longus and semitendinosus was higher on the contra vs. ipsilateral side in the UBI rats.
evidence: The claim is supported by EMG data and statistical analyses presented in Figure 2D showing a 5.9-fold higher number of spikes in the contralesional semitendinosus muscle.

claim: The threshold was lower for the contra vs. ipsilesional semitendinosus muscle in UBI rats with transected spinal cord.
source: Consistently, the threshold was lower for the contra vs. ipsilesional semitendinosus.
evidence: The claim is supported by EMG data and statistical analyses presented in Figure 2C showing a 3.6-fold lower threshold in the contralesional semitendinosus muscle.

claim: UBI markedly elevated the sensitivity of semitendinosus afferents on the contralesional vs. ipsilesional side in rats with transected spinal cord.
source: Regardless of mechanism, robust differences in the asymmetry index between the UBI and sham groups suggested that the UBI markedly elevated both the sensitivity of semitendinosus afferents and the excitability of the extensor digitorum longus and semitendinosus efferents, all on the contralesional vs. ipsilesional side.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the EMG data showing lower thresholds in the contralesional semitendinosus muscle, suggesting increased afferent sensitivity.

claim: UBI markedly elevated the excitability of the extensor digitorum longus efferents on the contralesional vs. ipsilesional side in rats with transected spinal cord.
source: Regardless of mechanism, robust differences in the asymmetry index between the UBI and sham groups suggested that the UBI markedly elevated both the sensitivity of semitendinosus afferents and the excitability of the extensor digitorum longus and semitendinosus efferents, all on the contralesional vs. ipsilesional side.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the EMG data showing increased spike numbers in the contralesional extensor digitorum longus muscle, suggesting increased efferent excitability.

claim: UBI markedly elevated the excitability of the semitendinosus efferents on the contralesional vs. ipsilesional side in rats with transected spinal cord.
source: Regardless of mechanism, robust differences in the asymmetry index between the UBI and sham groups suggested that the UBI markedly elevated both the sensitivity of semitendinosus afferents and the excitability of the extensor digitorum longus and semitendinosus efferents, all on the contralesional vs. ipsilesional side.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the EMG data showing increased spike numbers in the contralesional semitendinosus muscle, suggesting increased efferent excitability.

claim: UBI inhibited the contralesional interosseous muscle in rats with transected spinal cord.
source: The UBI also inhibited the contralesional interosseous.
evidence: The claim is supported by EMG data showing decreased asymmetry index for the interosseous muscle, suggesting inhibition on the contralesional side.

claim: The UBI effects on the hindlimb withdrawal reflexes in rats with transected spinal cords were similar to those of the UBI animals with intact spinal cords.
source: The UBI effects on the hindlimb withdrawal reflexes in rats with the transected spinal cords were similar in their range and contra-ipsilesional patterns to those of the UBI animals with intact spinal cords (Watanabe et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of current experimental data with previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: UBI effects on withdrawal reflexes corroborate clinical findings showing contralateral facilitation of withdrawal reflexes in stroke patients.
source: These effects corroborate clinical findings showing contralateral facilitation of withdrawal reflexes in stroke patients (Dewald et al., 1999; Serrao et al., 2012; Spaich et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim connects the experimental findings to clinical observations through citations to studies in stroke patients.

claim: The median gene expression asymmetry index of 19 out of 20 genes at the pairwise comparison was lower in the UBI rats compared to sham surgery group.
source: The median gene expression asymmetry index of 19 out of 20 genes at the pairwise comparison was lower in the UBI rats compared to sham surgery group (sign-test: p = 4×10−5) (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of gene expression data presented in Figure 3A,B showing a significant shift in asymmetry index across multiple genes.

claim: Changes in the gene expression asymmetry index were consistent with decreased expression of 17 genes in the contralesional half of the lumbar spinal cord after UBI.
source: Changes in the gene expression asymmetry index were consistent with decreased expression of 17 genes (sign test: p = 0.003) in the contralesional half (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D) concomitantly with elevated expression of 15 genes (sign test: p = 0.041) in the ipsilesional half (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of gene expression data showing a significant pattern of decreased expression in the contralesional spinal cord half.

claim: Changes in the gene expression asymmetry index were consistent with elevated expression of 15 genes in the ipsilesional half of the lumbar spinal cord after UBI.
source: Changes in the gene expression asymmetry index were consistent with decreased expression of 17 genes (sign test: p = 0.003) in the contralesional half (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D) concomitantly with elevated expression of 15 genes (sign test: p = 0.041) in the ipsilesional half (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of gene expression data showing a significant pattern of increased expression in the ipsilesional spinal cord half.

claim: The proportion of intra-area positive correlations in gene expression was reduced after UBI in the lumbar spinal cord.
source: The proportion of intra-area positive correlations, which dominated in rats with sham surgery, was reduced after the UBI (Fisher's Exact Test: all correlations in the right half, p = 3×10−5; significant correlations in the left and right areas, p = 0.008 and 0.009, respectively) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of gene expression data showing reduced positive correlations within spinal cord halves after UBI.

claim: The inter-area gene-gene coordination strength was decreased after UBI in the lumbar spinal cord.
source: The inter-area gene-gene coordination strength was decreased after the UBI (Wilcoxon signed-rank test; all and significant correlations: p = 4×10−7 and 3×10−4, respectively) (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis presented in Figure 3C,D showing decreased coordination of gene expression between left and right spinal cord halves after UBI.

claim: Positive inter-area correlations in gene expression were predominant in rats with sham surgery (68%) in contrast to the UBI rats (42%).
source: Positive inter-area correlations were predominant in rats with sham surgery (68%) in contrast to the UBI rats (42%) (Fisher's Exact Test: all and significant correlations, p = 6×10−14 and 0.004, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of correlation patterns showing a shift from predominantly positive to more negative correlations after UBI.

claim: UBI robustly impairs coordination of expression of neuroplasticity-related and neuropeptide genes within and between the left and right halves of the lumbar spinal cord.
source: Thus, the UBI robustly impairs coordination of expression of neuroplasticity-related and neuropeptide genes within and between the left and right halves of the lumbar spinal cord.
evidence: The claim is a summary interpretation of the gene expression correlation analyses showing disrupted coordination patterns after UBI.

claim: UBI substantially elevated the levels of Met-enkephalin-Arg-Phe in the ipsilesional lumbar spinal cord.
source: Fourth, analysis of opioid peptides demonstrated that the UBI substantially elevated the levels of the proenkephalin marker Met-enkephalin-Arg-Phe in the ipsilesional (Padjusted = 9×10−4) and contralesional (Punadjusted = 0.020) spinal halves (Figure 3E), and the prodynorphin-derived Dynorphin B and Leu-enkephalin-Arg in the ipsilesional spinal cord (for both, Punadjusted < 0.05) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by radioimmunoassay data presented in Figure 3E showing a 1.4-fold increase in Met-enkephalin-Arg-Phe levels in the ipsilesional spinal cord.

claim: UBI substantially elevated the levels of Met-enkephalin-Arg-Phe in the contralesional lumbar spinal cord.
source: Fourth, analysis of opioid peptides demonstrated that the UBI substantially elevated the levels of the proenkephalin marker Met-enkephalin-Arg-Phe in the ipsilesional (Padjusted = 9×10−4) and contralesional (Punadjusted = 0.020) spinal halves (Figure 3E), and the prodynorphin-derived Dynorphin B and Leu-enkephalin-Arg in the ipsilesional spinal cord (for both, Punadjusted < 0.05) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by radioimmunoassay data presented in Figure 3E showing a 1.3-fold increase in Met-enkephalin-Arg-Phe levels in the contralesional spinal cord.

claim: UBI elevated the levels of Dynorphin B in the ipsilesional lumbar spinal cord.
source: Fourth, analysis of opioid peptides demonstrated that the UBI substantially elevated the levels of the proenkephalin marker Met-enkephalin-Arg-Phe in the ipsilesional (Padjusted = 9×10−4) and contralesional (Punadjusted = 0.020) spinal halves (Figure 3E), and the prodynorphin-derived Dynorphin B and Leu-enkephalin-Arg in the ipsilesional spinal cord (for both, Punadjusted < 0.05) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by radioimmunoassay data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 showing increased Dynorphin B levels in the ipsilesional spinal cord.

claim: UBI elevated the levels of Leu-enkephalin-Arg in the ipsilesional lumbar spinal cord.
source: Fourth, analysis of opioid peptides demonstrated that the UBI substantially elevated the levels of the proenkephalin marker Met-enkephalin-Arg-Phe in the ipsilesional (Padjusted = 9×10−4) and contralesional (Punadjusted = 0.020) spinal halves (Figure 3E), and the prodynorphin-derived Dynorphin B and Leu-enkephalin-Arg in the ipsilesional spinal cord (for both, Punadjusted < 0.05) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by radioimmunoassay data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 showing increased Leu-enkephalin-Arg levels in the ipsilesional spinal cord.

claim: No HL-PA developed in hypophysectomized animals that received left UBI after spinal transection.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, no HL-PA developed in hypophysectomized animals that received left UBI after spinal transection (n = 8); the HL-PA median values and PA were nearly identical to those in sham operated rats (n = 8) (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4A showing that hypophysectomized rats did not develop hindlimb postural asymmetry after UBI.

claim: Serum collected 3 hr after performing a left UBI in rats with transected spinal cord induced HL-PA when administered centrally to rats after their spinalization.
source: Serum that was collected 3 hr after performing a left UBI in rats with transected spinal cord was administered either centrally (into the cisterna magna; UBI serum, n = 13; sham serum, n = 7; Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–J) or intravenously (UBI serum, n = 13; sham serum, n = 7; Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1K–O) to rats after their spinalization. Serum administration by either route resulted in formation of HL-PA with its values and its probability similar to those induced by the UBI in rats with intact and transected spinal cords.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F-J showing that intracisternal administration of UBI serum induced hindlimb postural asymmetry.

claim: Serum collected 3 hr after performing a left UBI in rats with transected spinal cord induced HL-PA when administered intravenously to rats after their spinalization.
source: Serum that was collected 3 hr after performing a left UBI in rats with transected spinal cord was administered either centrally (into the cisterna magna; UBI serum, n = 13; sham serum, n = 7; Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–J) or intravenously (UBI serum, n = 13; sham serum, n = 7; Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1K–O) to rats after their spinalization. Serum administration by either route resulted in formation of HL-PA with its values and its probability similar to those induced by the UBI in rats with intact and transected spinal cords.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4B showing that intravenous administration of UBI serum induced hindlimb postural asymmetry.

claim: Animals injected with serum from rats with left UBI displayed hindlimb flexion on the right side, which was the same as the flexion side in the donor rats.
source: Remarkably, animals injected with serum from rats with left UBI displayed hindlimb flexion on the right side, which was the same as the flexion side in the donor rats (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–O).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that serum transfer preserved the side-specific pattern of hindlimb flexion corresponding to the donor's brain injury side.

claim: No HL-PA developed after administration of serum collected from rats with left sham surgery.
source: No HL-PA developed after administration of serum collected from rats with the left sham surgery.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that sham surgery serum did not induce hindlimb postural asymmetry, serving as a control for the UBI serum experiments.

claim: The left UBI stimulates a release of chemical factors from the pituitary gland into the blood that induce HL-PA with contralesional flexion.
source: We conclude that the left UBI stimulates a release of chemical factors from the pituitary gland into the blood that induce HL-PA with contralesional flexion.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the combined findings that hypophysectomy abolishes UBI effects and that serum from UBI rats can induce hindlimb postural asymmetry in naive animals.

claim: Arg-vasopressin administered intracisternally induced flexion of the right hindlimb.
source: Here, we first replicated the effects of Arg-vasopressin that, consistent with a previous study (Klement'ev et al., 1986), produced flexion of the right hindlimb after its intracisternal administration (Figure 4—figure supplement 2; peptide, n = 22, and saline, n = 9 at the 180 min time point).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 showing that intracisternal Arg-vasopressin administration induced right hindlimb flexion.

claim: Intravenous injection of β-endorphin to rats with transected spinal cords resulted in development of HL-PA with right hindlimb flexion.
source: Injection of these neurohormones, but not saline, to rats with transected spinal cords resulted in development of HL-PA with right hindlimb flexion (Figure 4C; β-endorphin, n = 8; Arg-vasopressin, n = 7; saline, n = 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4C showing that intravenous β-endorphin administration induced hindlimb postural asymmetry with right hindlimb flexion.

claim: Intravenous injection of Arg-vasopressin to rats with transected spinal cords resulted in development of HL-PA with right hindlimb flexion.
source: Injection of these neurohormones, but not saline, to rats with transected spinal cords resulted in development of HL-PA with right hindlimb flexion (Figure 4C; β-endorphin, n = 8; Arg-vasopressin, n = 7; saline, n = 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4C showing that intravenous Arg-vasopressin administration induced hindlimb postural asymmetry with right hindlimb flexion.

claim: Naloxone inhibited HL-PA formation in UBI rats with transected spinal cord.
source: Naloxone and SSR-149415, the opioid and vasopressin V1B receptor antagonists, respectively, administered to animals with transected spinal cord that also received a left UBI (naloxone, n = 6; SSR-149415, n = 6; saline and vehicle, n = 11) inhibited HL-PA formation (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4D showing that naloxone administration blocked hindlimb postural asymmetry formation after UBI.

claim: SSR-149415 inhibited HL-PA formation in UBI rats with transected spinal cord.
source: Naloxone and SSR-149415, the opioid and vasopressin V1B receptor antagonists, respectively, administered to animals with transected spinal cord that also received a left UBI (naloxone, n = 6; SSR-149415, n = 6; saline and vehicle, n = 11) inhibited HL-PA formation (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4D showing that SSR-149415 administration blocked hindlimb postural asymmetry formation after UBI.

claim: The HL-PA induced by serum from animals with left UBI was abolished by administration of naloxone.
source: Similarly, the HL-PA induced by serum from animals with left UBI was abolished by administration of either naloxone (n = 6) or SSR-149415 (n = 6) (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4E showing that naloxone blocked hindlimb postural asymmetry induced by UBI serum.

claim: The HL-PA induced by serum from animals with left UBI was abolished by administration of SSR-149415.
source: Similarly, the HL-PA induced by serum from animals with left UBI was abolished by administration of either naloxone (n = 6) or SSR-149415 (n = 6) (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4E showing that SSR-149415 blocked hindlimb postural asymmetry induced by UBI serum.

claim: The pituitary neurohormones β-endorphin and Arg-vasopressin released into the systemic circulation may serve as side-specific signals that mediate UBI effects on hindlimb motor circuits.
source: Thus, the pituitary neurohormones β-endorphin and Arg-vasopressin released into the systemic circulation may serve as side-specific signals that mediate UBI effects on hindlimb motor circuits.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the combined findings that these neurohormones induce side-specific hindlimb responses, their effects are blocked by receptor antagonists, and hypophysectomy abolishes UBI effects.

claim: Functional lateralization is an organizing principle in the adult brain.
source: In the adult brain, functional lateralization is an organizing principle (Duboc et al., 2015; MacNeilage et al., 2009) and lateralized functions may be regulated by paracrine signaling molecules including peptide neurohormones (Deliagina et al., 2000; Hussain et al., 2012; Kononenko et al., 2017; Marlin et al., 2015; Nation et al., 2018; Phelps et al., 2019; Watanabe et al., 2015; Watanabe et al., 2021; Zink et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature on brain lateralization and its regulation.

claim: Oxytocin enables retrieval behavior by enhancing responses of the left, but not right, auditory cortex through its receptors expressed on the left side.
source: Thus, oxytocin enables retrieval behavior by enhancing responses of the left, but not right, auditory cortex through its receptors expressed on the left side (Marlin et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study by Marlin et al., 2015 demonstrating lateralized effects of oxytocin.

claim: Arg-vasopressin targets the left but not right hemispheric areas to modulate social recognition-related activity.
source: Arg-vasopressin targets the left but not right hemispheric areas to modulate social recognition-related activity (Zink et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study by Zink et al., 2011 demonstrating lateralized effects of Arg-vasopressin.

claim: Asymmetric distribution of the μ-opioid receptor along with opioid peptides may provide a basis for the lateralized processing of positive and negative emotions in the human brain.
source: In the human brain, asymmetric distribution of the μ-opioid receptor along with opioid peptides that elicit euphoria and dysphoria may provide a basis for the lateralized processing of positive and negative emotions (Kantonen et al., 2020; Watanabe et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating asymmetric distribution of opioid receptors and their role in emotional processing.

claim: Top-down control of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis is left-right hemisphere specific.
source: Top-down control of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal and hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axes, as well as the immune system, is left-right hemisphere specific (Bakalkin et al., 1984; Inase and Machida, 1992; Kiss et al., 2020; Lueken et al., 2009; Madsen et al., 2012; Meador et al., 2004; Sullivan and Gratton, 2002; Xavier et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies demonstrating lateralized control of neuroendocrine systems.

claim: Top-down control of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis is left-right hemisphere specific.
source: Top-down control of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal and hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axes, as well as the immune system, is left-right hemisphere specific (Bakalkin et al., 1984; Inase and Machida, 1992; Kiss et al., 2020; Lueken et al., 2009; Madsen et al., 2012; Meador et al., 2004; Sullivan and Gratton, 2002; Xavier et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies demonstrating lateralized control of neuroendocrine systems.

claim: Top-down control of the immune system is left-right hemisphere specific.
source: Top-down control of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal and hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axes, as well as the immune system, is left-right hemisphere specific (Bakalkin et al., 1984; Inase and Machida, 1992; Kiss et al., 2020; Lueken et al., 2009; Madsen et al., 2012; Meador et al., 2004; Sullivan and Gratton, 2002; Xavier et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies demonstrating lateralized control of the immune system.

claim: Right-sided injuries to the brain or spinal nerves compared to those on the left side produce stronger effects on the neuroendocrine systems.
source: The right-sided injuries to the brain or spinal nerves compared to those on the left side produce stronger effects on the neuroendocrine systems, including hormonal levels in the peripheral circulation (Hussain et al., 2012; Inase and Machida, 1992; Kononenko et al., 2017; Lueken et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating asymmetric neuroendocrine responses to lateralized injuries.

claim: Cortisol secretion is under excitatory control of the right hemisphere.
source: Cortisol (corticosterone) secretion is under excitatory control of the right hemisphere and, consistently, its phasic response is diminished in patients with right but not left sided stroke (Lueken et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study by Lueken et al., 2009 demonstrating lateralized control of cortisol secretion.

claim: Basal and corticotropin-releasing hormone–induced secretion of Arg-vasopressin and ACTH by the pituitary gland is lateralized to the right petrosal sinus.
source: Thus, basal and corticotropin-releasing hormone–induced secretion of Arg-vasopressin and ACTH by the pituitary gland is lateralized to the right petrosal sinus (Kalogeras et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study by Kalogeras et al., 1996 demonstrating lateralized pituitary hormone secretion.

claim: Non-directional stimuli such as stress and stress-induced pain produce lateralized responses in the CNS.
source: Conversely, non-directional stimuli such as stress and stress-induced pain produce lateralized responses in the CNS (Bakalkin et al., 1982; Bakalkin et al., 1984; Nation et al., 2018; Sullivan and Gratton, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating lateralized CNS responses to non-directional stimuli.

claim: Both left- and right-sided nerve or body injuries elicit functional and molecular responses that are often lateralized to the right in the brain and spinal cord.
source: Both left- and right-sided nerve or body injuries elicit functional and molecular responses that are often lateralized to the right, but not to the left, in the brain and spinal cord (Bakalkin et al., 1984; Hussain et al., 2012; Inase and Machida, 1992; Kononenko et al., 2017; Phelps et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating right-lateralized responses to injuries regardless of injury side.

claim: Neuropathic pain induced by either the left- or right-sided nerve injuries is controlled through κ-opioid receptors in the right amygdala.
source: Neuropathic pain induced by either the left- or right-sided nerve injuries is controlled through κ-opioid receptors in the right amygdala (Phelps et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study by Phelps et al., 2019 demonstrating lateralized pain control mechanisms.

claim: Encoding of information about the injury side in a hormonal message, humoral transmission of this message to its target sites, and translation of this message into the left-right side-specific response are the key stages of left-right side-specific humoral signaling.
source: Encoding of information about the injury side in a hormonal message, humoral transmission of this message to its target sites on peripheral nerve endings or spinal neurons, and translation of this message into the left-right side-specific response, are the key stages of this phenomenon.
evidence: The claim is a conceptual framework proposed by the authors to explain the mechanism of side-specific humoral signaling based on their experimental findings.

claim: Peptide neurohormones and opioids administered intravenously, intrathecally or intracisternally induce HL-PA in rats with intact brain.
source: Together with previous reports (Bakalkin et al., 1981; Bakalkin and Kobylyansky, 1989; Bakalkin et al., 1986; Chazov et al., 1981; Watanabe et al., 2020), this study demonstrates that peptide neurohormones and opioids administered intravenously, intrathecally or intracisternally induce HL-PA in rats with intact brain.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and experimental data in the current manuscript.

claim: The side of the flexed limb depends on the compound administered in neurohormone-induced HL-PA.
source: The critical finding is that the side of the flexed limb depends on the compound administered.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that different neurohormones induce flexion of different hindlimbs.

claim: Endogenous and synthetic κ-opioid agonists dynorphin, bremazocine, and U-50,488 induce flexion of the left hindlimb.
source: Endogenous and synthetic κ-opioid agonists dynorphin, bremazocine, and U-50,488, along with the endogenous μ/δ-opioid agonist Met-enkephalin, induce flexion of the left hindlimb (Bakalkin et al., 1981; Bakalkin and Kobylyansky, 1989; Bakalkin et al., 1986; Chazov et al., 1981; Watanabe et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating side-specific effects of κ-opioid agonists.

claim: β-endorphin causes the right limb to flex.
source: In contrast, β-endorphin and Arg-vasopressin, and the δ-agonist Leu-enkephalin, cause the right limb to flex [the present study and Bakalkin et al., 1981; Chazov et al., 1981; Klement'ev et al., 1986].
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in the current study and citations to previous studies.

claim: Topographical information conveyed by 'non-directional' molecular messengers circulating in the blood is converted into side-specific motor responses.
source: Thus, topographical information conveyed by the 'non-directional' molecular messengers circulating in the blood is converted into side-specific motor responses.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental findings that systemically administered neurohormones induce side-specific motor responses.

claim: Hypophysectomy disables the endocrine pathway including its opioid and Arg-vasopressin components and abolishes the HL-PA.
source: Hypophysectomy disables the endocrine pathway including its opioid and Arg-vasopressin components and abolishes the HL-PA.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that hypophysectomized rats did not develop hindlimb postural asymmetry after UBI.

claim: Serum from rats with left UBI induces HL-PA with contralesional hindlimb flexion in rats with intact brain.
source: Consistent with this finding, serum from rats with left UBI induces HL-PA with contralesional hindlimb flexion in rats with intact brain.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that serum transfer from UBI rats to naive rats induced hindlimb postural asymmetry.

claim: The pituitary gland is the main source of Arg-vasopressin and β-endorphin in the body that are secreted into the bloodstream.
source: The pituitary gland is the main source of Arg-vasopressin and β-endorphin in the body that are secreted into the bloodstream (Autelitano et al., 1989; Day and Akil, 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on pituitary hormone secretion and represents established knowledge in neuroendocrinology.

claim: Naloxone and SSR-149415 block the left UBI-induced formation of HL-PA.
source: Naloxone and SSR-149415 block the left UBI-induced formation of HL-PA.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that these receptor antagonists prevented hindlimb postural asymmetry formation after UBI.

claim: Opioid and Arg-vasopressin neurohormones transmit side-specific signals from the injured brain to the spinal neural circuits.
source: Altogether, these findings demonstrate that opioid and Arg-vasopressin neurohormones transmit side-specific signals from the injured brain to the spinal neural circuits.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the combined findings from hypophysectomy, serum transfer, neurohormone administration, and receptor antagonist experiments.

claim: Stroke or traumatic brain injury causes robust functional changes in contralateral withdrawal reflexes.
source: Clinical studies revealed robust functional changes induced by stroke or traumatic brain injury (TBI) in contralateral withdrawal reflexes that also control posture and locomotion (Dewald et al., 1999; Sandrini et al., 2005; Serrao et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to clinical studies demonstrating changes in withdrawal reflexes after brain injury.

claim: Patients with post-stroke motor deficits lose their ability to modulate the withdrawal reflexes.
source: Patients with post-stroke motor deﬁcits lose their ability to modulate the withdrawal reflexes that affects spatiotemporal interaction among joints and causes movement abnormalities during motor activities (Bohannon and Smith, 1987; Serrao et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to clinical studies on post-stroke motor deficits.

claim: Spinal withdrawal reflexes are regulated by endogenous opioid peptides that may suppress the ipsilateral and contralateral segmental reflexes.
source: Spinal withdrawal reflexes are regulated by the endogenous opioid peptides that may suppress the ipsilateral and contralateral segmental reflexes (Clarke et al., 1992; Duarte et al., 2019; Jankowska and Schomburg, 1998; Schmidt et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating opioid regulation of spinal reflexes.

claim: Opioid receptors are expressed both in the dorsal and ventral horns of the spinal cord.
source: Opioid receptors are expressed both in the dorsal and ventral horns of the spinal cord (Kononenko et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018) and also in the periphery, in primary afferents including low-threshold mechanoreceptors that modulate cutaneous mechanosensation (Bardoni et al., 2014; Snyder et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating the distribution of opioid receptors in the spinal cord.

claim: Opioid receptors are expressed in the periphery, in primary afferents including low-threshold mechanoreceptors that modulate cutaneous mechanosensation.
source: Opioid receptors are expressed both in the dorsal and ventral horns of the spinal cord (Kononenko et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018) and also in the periphery, in primary afferents including low-threshold mechanoreceptors that modulate cutaneous mechanosensation (Bardoni et al., 2014; Snyder et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating peripheral expression of opioid receptors.

claim: A large fraction of patients with stroke and cerebral palsy have tonically contracted muscles without any voluntary command, a phenomenon called 'spastic dystonia'.
source: A large fraction of patients with stroke and cerebral palsy do not relax their muscles – they are tonically contracted without any voluntary command (Baude et al., 2019; Gracies, 2005; Lorentzen et al., 2018; Sheean and McGuire, 2009; Trompetto et al., 2019). This phenomenon is called 'spastic dystonia' and has a central mechanism that does not depend on afferent input (Gracies, 2005; Lorentzen et al., 2018; Sheean and McGuire, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to clinical studies on spastic dystonia in stroke and cerebral palsy patients.

claim: Spastic dystonia has a central mechanism that does not depend on afferent input.
source: A large fraction of patients with stroke and cerebral palsy do not relax their muscles – they are tonically contracted without any voluntary command (Baude et al., 2019; Gracies, 2005; Lorentzen et al., 2018; Sheean and McGuire, 2009; Trompetto et al., 2019). This phenomenon is called 'spastic dystonia' and has a central mechanism that does not depend on afferent input (Gracies, 2005; Lorentzen et al., 2018; Sheean and McGuire, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to clinical studies on the mechanisms of spastic dystonia.

claim: HL-PA is resistant to bilateral lumbar dorsal rhizotomy.
source: The finding that HL-PA is resistant to bilateral lumbar dorsal rhizotomy (Zhang et al., 2020) further supports this notion and suggests that the HL-PA and the clinical 'spastic dystonia' may be mechanistically similar.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors demonstrating that HL-PA persists after dorsal rhizotomy.

claim: The HL-PA and the clinical 'spastic dystonia' may be mechanistically similar.
source: The finding that HL-PA is resistant to bilateral lumbar dorsal rhizotomy (Zhang et al., 2020) further supports this notion and suggests that the HL-PA and the clinical 'spastic dystonia' may be mechanistically similar.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on similarities between HL-PA and spastic dystonia, both being independent of afferent input.

claim: Classical hyperreflexia develops during several weeks after the impact and is considered as pathology of the corticospinal tract.
source: Classical hyperreflexia develops during several weeks after the impact and is considered as pathology of the corticospinal tract (Williams et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study on hyperreflexia development after spinal cord injury.

claim: The HL-PA is formed within 30 min after the UBI in rats with transected spinal cord.
source: In contrast, the HL-PA is formed within 30 min after the UBI in rats with transected spinal cord.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing rapid development of hindlimb postural asymmetry after UBI.

claim: Single injection of either naloxone or SSR-149415 inhibited HL-PA asymmetry formation.
source: Single injection of either naloxone or SSR-149415 inhibited HL-PA asymmetry formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that single doses of these antagonists blocked hindlimb postural asymmetry.

claim: The vasopressin receptor V1B is largely expressed in the anterior pituitary by corticotrophs producing proopiomelanocortin.
source: The vasopressin receptor V1B is largely expressed in the anterior pituitary by corticotrophs producing proopiomelanocortin (Roper et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study on vasopressin receptor expression in the pituitary.

claim: Arg-vasopressin released from neurohypophysis may activate the V1B receptor and stimulate secretion of proopiomelanocortin-derived β-endorphin.
source: A plausible scenario is that Arg-vasopressin released from neurohypophysis activates the V1B receptor and stimulates secretion of proopiomelanocortin-derived β-endorphin (Roper et al., 2011) that induces the HL-PA.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the mechanism by which Arg-vasopressin might induce HL-PA, based on known receptor interactions.

claim: Arg-vasopressin and β-endorphin may produce synergistic effects acting through the complex of the vasopressin receptor V1B and μ-opioid receptor.
source: Alternatively, Arg-vasopressin and β-endorphin may produce synergistic effects acting through the complex of the vasopressin receptor V1B and μ-opioid receptor that integrates two signaling pathways (Koshimizu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is a speculation about an alternative mechanism based on known receptor interactions, supported by citation.

claim: The general opioid antagonists naloxone and naltrexone may normalize neurological functions that are impaired in animals and human patients after unilateral cerebral ischemia.
source: The general opioid antagonists naloxone and naltrexone may normalize neurological functions that are impaired in animals and human patients after unilateral cerebral ischemia (Baskin and Hosobuchi, 1981; Baskin et al., 1984; Baskin et al., 1994; Hans et al., 1992; Hosobuchi et al., 1982; Jabaily and Davis, 1984; Namba et al., 1986; Skarphedinsson et al., 1989; Wang et al., 2019), and also reduce spasticity in patients with primary progressive multiple sclerosis (Gironi et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple clinical and preclinical studies on the therapeutic effects of opioid antagonists.

claim: Naloxone and naltrexone reduce spasticity in patients with primary progressive multiple sclerosis.
source: The general opioid antagonists naloxone and naltrexone may normalize neurological functions that are impaired in animals and human patients after unilateral cerebral ischemia (Baskin and Hosobuchi, 1981; Baskin et al., 1984; Baskin et al., 1994; Hans et al., 1992; Hosobuchi et al., 1982; Jabaily and Davis, 1984; Namba et al., 1986; Skarphedinsson et al., 1989; Wang et al., 2019), and also reduce spasticity in patients with primary progressive multiple sclerosis (Gironi et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a clinical study on the effects of opioid antagonists in multiple sclerosis.

claim: The efficacy of pharmacological treatment may depend on topographical correspondence between the side of neuronal deficits and the side that is preferentially targeted by neurohormones and their antagonists.
source: Our findings suggest that the efficacy of pharmacological treatment may depend on topographical correspondence between the side of neuronal deficits and the side that is preferentially targeted by neurohormones and their antagonists.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about clinical implications based on the experimental findings of side-specific neurohormonal effects.

claim: Three-quarters of cervical spinal cords are asymmetric with a larger right side.
source: Three-quarters of cervical spinal cords are asymmetric with a larger right side (Nathan et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to an anatomical study on spinal cord asymmetry.

claim: Spinal-muscular systems are asymmetric in human fetuses, and the asymmetry correlates with lateralized gene transcription.
source: Spinal-muscular systems are asymmetric in human fetuses, and the asymmetry correlates with lateralized gene transcription (de Kovel et al., 2017; Ocklenburg et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on developmental asymmetry in spinal-muscular systems.

claim: Mono- and polysynaptic segmental reflexes evoked by stimulation of the dorsal roots and recorded in the ventral roots in intact rats and cats display higher activity on the right side.
source: Mono- and polysynaptic segmental reflexes evoked by stimulation of the dorsal roots and recorded in the ventral roots in intact rats and cats display higher activity on the right side (Hultborn and Malmsten, 1983a; Hultborn and Malmsten, 1983b; Malmsten, 1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to electrophysiological studies demonstrating asymmetric spinal reflexes.

claim: EMG recordings of hindlimb withdrawal reflexes evoked by electrical stimulation in control rats display higher activity on the right side.
source: Similarly, EMG recordings of hindlimb withdrawal reflexes evoked by electrical stimulation in control rats display higher activity on the right side (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors demonstrating asymmetric withdrawal reflexes.

claim: In the rat spinal cord, the expression of three opioid receptors is lateralized to the left.
source: In the rat spinal cord, the expression of three opioid receptors is lateralized to the left, and their proportions and co-expression patterns are different between the left and right sides (Kononenko et al., 2017; Watanabe et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors demonstrating lateralized opioid receptor expression.

claim: The proportions and co-expression patterns of opioid receptors are different between the left and right sides of the rat spinal cord.
source: In the rat spinal cord, the expression of three opioid receptors is lateralized to the left, and their proportions and co-expression patterns are different between the left and right sides (Kononenko et al., 2017; Watanabe et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors demonstrating asymmetric opioid receptor co-expression patterns.

claim: The asymmetry may be a critical feature of the spinal cord allowing translation of the 'non-directional' hormonal messages into the left-right side-specific response.
source: The asymmetry may be a critical feature of the spinal cord allowing translation of the 'non-directional' hormonal messages into the left-right side-specific response.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the functional significance of spinal cord asymmetry based on the experimental findings.

claim: The side-specific endocrine signaling was revealed in anaesthetized animals with transected spinal cords that were studied up to 180 min post UBI.
source: The side-specific endocrine signaling was revealed in anaesthetized animals with transected spinal cords that were studied up to 180 min post UBI.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental conditions under which the findings were obtained, acknowledging limitations of the study.

claim: Forelimb postural asymmetry was not induced by lesion of the hindlimb sensorimotor cortex.
source: The study did not analyze forelimb postural asymmetry. It was not induced by lesion of the hindlimb sensorimotor cortex (Zhang et al., 2020) but it did develop after injury of the forelimb area (unpublished data).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study and reference to unpublished data.

claim: Forelimb postural asymmetry developed after injury of the forelimb area.
source: The study did not analyze forelimb postural asymmetry. It was not induced by lesion of the hindlimb sensorimotor cortex (Zhang et al., 2020) but it did develop after injury of the forelimb area (unpublished data).
evidence: The claim is based on unpublished data mentioned by the authors.

claim: Rats with intact and transected spinal cords developed HL-PA during the first 30 min following UBI.
source: Rats with intact (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D) and transected (Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4) spinal cords developed HL-PA during the first 30 min following UBI.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the time course of HL-PA development in both groups.

claim: TBI and stroke cause dysfunction of the hypothalamic–pituitary system and hypopituitarism manifested as changes in secretion of pituitary hormones.
source: TBI and stroke cause dysfunction of the hypothalamic–pituitary system and hypopituitarism manifested as changes in secretion of pituitary hormones (Bondanelli et al., 2005; Emelifeonwu et al., 2020; Klose and Feldt-Rasmussen, 2018; Lillicrap et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to clinical studies on neuroendocrine dysfunction after brain injury.

claim: Ischemic stroke activates the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal axis.
source: Ischemic stroke activates the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal axis (Anne et al., 2007), while a unilateral ablation of sensorimotor cortex elevates the level of circulating ACTH and induces morphological changes in the pituitary corticotrophs that produce ACTH and β-endorphin (Lavrnja et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study on neuroendocrine responses to stroke.

claim: A unilateral ablation of sensorimotor cortex elevates the level of circulating ACTH and induces morphological changes in the pituitary corticotrophs.
source: Ischemic stroke activates the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal axis (Anne et al., 2007), while a unilateral ablation of sensorimotor cortex elevates the level of circulating ACTH and induces morphological changes in the pituitary corticotrophs that produce ACTH and β-endorphin (Lavrnja et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study on pituitary responses to cortical ablation.

claim: Cortical projections to the hypothalamus may potentially mediate effects of focal brain injury on secretion of pituitary hormones.
source: However, cortical projections to the hypothalamus that may potentially mediate effects of focal brain injury on secretion of pituitary hormones have been described (Jeong et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study on cortical-hypothalamic projections, suggesting a potential anatomical pathway.
